record.original_question: In the regime where the dimension d is larger than polylogarithmic in 1/epsilon but smaller than polynomial in 1/epsilon, and only essentially linear memory is available between oracle calls, can convex L-Lipschitz optimization be solved with a number of first-order queries that is polynomial in d? More specifically, when the memory budget satisfies M = Theta(d polylog(LB/epsilon)) or M = O~(d), is T(d,M,epsilon) = O(poly d) achievable in that intermediate scaling regime?

evidence.quote: Therefore, as a starting point, we ask to characterize T(d, Theta(d polylog LB/epsilon), 1/epsilon). In particular, is it possible to have query complexity polynomial in d with O~(d) memory?
Question 2 ($200 or One Star Michelin Meal) Can we have T(d, M = O~(d), epsilon) = O(poly d) when d = Omega(log^c 1/epsilon) but d = O(1/epsilon^c) for all c?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $B \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be the Euclidean unit ball and let $\mathcal{F}_{L,B}$ denote the class of convex, $L$-Lipschitz functions $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$. A first-order optimization algorithm interacts with an oracle that, given a query point $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, returns the pair $(f(x), g)$ for some subgradient $g \in \partial f(x)$. The algorithm is constrained so that, between consecutive oracle queries, it may store at most $M$ bits of working memory (the query point itself is recomputed from this state).

Define $T(d, M, \varepsilon)$ to be the smallest integer $T$ such that there exists a (possibly randomized) first-order algorithm using at most $M$ bits of memory between queries which, for every $f\in\mathcal{F}_{L,B}$, after at most $T$ oracle queries outputs a point $\hat x \in B$ satisfying
$$ \mathbb{E}[f(\hat x)] - \min_{x\in B} f(x) \le \varepsilon. $$

Consider the regime in which the dimension scales with the accuracy as
$$ d = \Omega(\log^c(1/\varepsilon)) \quad\text{for every constant } c>0, \qquad d = O((1/\varepsilon)^c) \quad\text{for every constant } c>0, $$
i.e. $d$ grows faster than any polylogarithm in $1/\varepsilon$ but slower than any polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$.

Question: With memory budget $M = \widetilde{O}(d)$ (in particular $M = \Theta(d \cdot \mathrm{polylog}(LB/\varepsilon))$, where $B$ is the radius bound), is it possible to achieve
$$ T(d, M, \varepsilon) = \mathrm{poly}(d)\,? $$
That is, characterize $T(d,\Theta(d\,\mathrm{polylog}(LB/\varepsilon)),1/\varepsilon)$ in this intermediate scaling regime, and determine whether a query complexity polynomial in $d$ is achievable with essentially linear memory.
artifact.status_search_result: The original open problem asks whether linear-memory first-order algorithms can solve convex Lipschitz optimization with poly(d) queries. Marsden, Sharan, Sidford and Valiant (2022) proved that any first-order algorithm using at most d^{1.25-δ} bits of memory must make Ω̃(d^{1+(4/3)δ}) queries to achieve 1/poly(d) accuracy, showing that linear-memory algorithms cannot match the Õ(d) cutting-plane query complexity and giving the first super-linear lower bound. Subsequent works (Blanchard–Zhang–Jaillet 2023; Chen–Peng 2023) gave further memory-query tradeoffs and recursive cutting-plane upper bounds. However, the precise question of whether T(d, Õ(d), ε) = poly(d) in the stated intermediate regime is not fully resolved: known lower bounds rule out this for low accuracy regimes but a tight characterization across the full intermediate scaling remains open.

status_evidence.title: Efficient Convex Optimization Requires Superlinear Memory
status_evidence.snippet: Any memory-constrained first-order algorithm minimizing d-dimensional 1-Lipschitz convex functions to 1/poly(d) accuracy using at most d^{1.25-δ} bits of memory must make Ω̃(d^{1+(4/3)δ}) queries; resolves the COLT 2019 open problem.
status_evidence.claim: Provides a superlinear-memory lower bound, partially resolving the open question by ruling out poly(d) queries with linear memory at high accuracy.

status_evidence.title: Memory-Constrained Algorithms for Convex Optimization via Recursive Cutting-Planes
status_evidence.snippet: Recursive cutting-plane algorithms achieve memory O(d^2/p log 1/ε) and O((Cd/p log 1/ε)^p) oracle calls, giving sub-polynomial-regime tradeoffs.
status_evidence.claim: Provides upper-bound tradeoffs relevant to the intermediate memory regime.

status_evidence.title: Memory-Query Tradeoffs for Randomized Convex Optimization
status_evidence.snippet: Any randomized first-order algorithm must use Ω(d^{2-δ}) memory or make Ω(d^{1+δ/6-o(1)}) queries.
status_evidence.claim: Strengthens lower bounds across memory regimes.
